etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English adjectif, adjective, from Old French adjectif, from Latin adiectivus, from adiciō + -īvus, from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + iaciō (“throw”). The Latin word adiectivus in turn was a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπιθετικόν (epithetikón, “added”), a derivative of the compound verb ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi), from which also comes epithet.

definitions.definition: (grammar) A word that modifies a noun  or noun phrase or describes a noun’s referent.

quote.citation: 1932, Delos W. Lovelace, King Kong, published 1965, page 8:
quote.text: "They'll have to invent new adjectives when I come back. You wait!"

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The History of the University of Cambridge, since the Conquest, [London]: [[…]  Iohn Williams […]], →OCLC:
quote.text: it must be an adjective of dain

definitions.definition: (grammar) Adjectival; pertaining to or functioning as an adjective.
(law) Applying to methods of enforcement and rules of procedure.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter X, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: The whole English law, substantive and adjective.

definitions.definition: (chemistry, of a dye) Needing the use of a mordant to be made fast to that which is being dyed.
(obsolete, reflected in the chemical sense, but extinct as a general sense) Incapable of independent function.

quote.citation: 1899, John Jay Chapman, Emerson and Other Essays, AMS Press (1969) (as reproduced in Project Gutenberg)
quote.text: In fact, God is of not so much importance in Himself, but as the end towards which man tends. That irreverent person who said that Browning uses “God” as a pigment made an accurate criticism of his theology. In Browning, God is adjective to man.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make an adjective of; to form or convert into an adjective.

quote.citation: 1805, John Horne Tooke, Epea Pteroenta: or The Diversions of Purley Part 2
quote.text: Language has as much occasion to adjective the distinct signification of the verb, and to adjective also the mood, as it has to adjective time. It has  […]  adjectived all three.

quote.citation: 1832, William Hunter, An Anglo-Saxon grammar, and derivatives, page 46:
quote.text: In English, instead of adjectiving our own substantives, we have borrowed, in immense numbers, adjectived signs from other languages […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, chiefly as a participle) To characterize with an adjective; to describe by using an adjective.
